Question: Do you maintain a documented AI policy, approved by senior management, that defines acceptable and prohibited uses of AI in your products?
Why it matters: Shows AI risk is owned at leadership level rather than left to individual product teams.

Question: Is a named role or committee accountable for AI risk, with authority to block or delay a release?
Why it matters: Accountability without the power to stop a release is advisory only.
Evidence requested: Org chart; committee charter; example of a blocked or delayed release

Question: Do you maintain an inventory of the AI models and features in the service you provide to us, including intended purpose and risk classification?
Why it matters: You cannot assess what the vendor itself has not catalogued.
Evidence requested: Inventory extract for the in-scope service

Question: Have you assessed your obligations under applicable AI regulation (e.g. the EU AI Act) for this service, including prohibited practices and whether you are the provider of a high-risk AI system?
Why it matters: Determines which obligations the vendor carries and which fall to us as deployer.

Question: Is customer data (inputs, outputs, uploaded files) used to train or fine-tune any model, including models that serve other customers? Is this on or off by default?
Why it matters: The most common unassessed AI risk: confidential data leaving the contractual boundary through model weights.
Evidence requested: Data use terms; description of opt-out and its default setting

Question: What is the retention period for prompts, inputs and model outputs, and can we configure it?
Why it matters: Prompts and outputs often contain personal data and fall outside standard retention schedules.

Question: Describe the provenance of training data for models used in the service, including third-party or scraped datasets and your rights to use them.
Why it matters: Unclear provenance creates IP, privacy and bias exposure that transfers to the customer.

Question: How do you assess whether training and evaluation data represent the populations the service will be used on?
Why it matters: A model trained on one population can systematically underperform on another.
Evidence requested: Data quality assessment; demographic coverage analysis

Question: Which third-party foundation models or AI services does the service depend on, and are they listed as sub-processors?
Why it matters: AI vendors often depend on an upstream model provider: a fourth party the customer never assessed.
Evidence requested: Sub-processor list; architecture diagram showing model calls

Question: Do you pin upstream model versions, and how are customers notified when an upstream model changes?
Why it matters: An upstream model update can change outputs overnight with no change on the vendor's side.

Question: Have you assessed your upstream model providers' security, data handling and acceptable-use terms?
Why it matters: The vendor's assurance is only as strong as its own third-party risk management over model providers.
Evidence requested: Vendor's assessment of model providers; contract extracts

Question: What is your contingency if an upstream model provider becomes unavailable or changes its terms?
Why it matters: Concentration risk: many AI services rely on the same few model providers.

Question: Which accuracy and performance metrics do you measure for the features we will use, and what were the most recent results?
Why it matters: Without stated metrics there is no baseline against which to detect degradation.

Question: Do you test for disparate performance or outcomes across demographic groups? Which groups, which metrics, and how often?
Why it matters: Essential for any system that influences decisions about people; a one-time pre-launch test is not enough.
Evidence requested: Bias testing methodology; most recent results

Question: Were evaluations performed on data representative of our geography, languages and use case?
Why it matters: Results from one market do not automatically transfer to another.

Question: Has an independent party reviewed or audited the model's performance or fairness?
Why it matters: Self-attestation on fairness is weak evidence.

Question: How do you protect against prompt injection, including indirect injection through documents or web content the model processes?
Why it matters: A leading attack class for LLM-based services that traditional security questionnaires do not cover.

Question: Can model outputs or agent actions reach systems or data beyond the requesting user's permissions?
Why it matters: Agentic features can turn a model error into an unauthorized action.
Evidence requested: Permission model for AI features; tool-access design

Question: Do you conduct adversarial testing (red-teaming) of AI features before release and on a recurring basis?
Why it matters: Standard penetration tests rarely cover model-specific abuse.

Question: How do you prevent one customer's data from appearing in another customer's outputs, including through shared models or caches?
Why it matters: Shared models and caches create cross-tenant leakage paths unique to AI.

Question: What documentation do you provide on intended use, limitations and known failure modes?
Why it matters: Deployers cannot oversee a system whose limits they do not know. Required of high-risk AI providers under the EU AI Act.

Question: Which features take or trigger actions without human review, and can customers disable them?
Why it matters: Automating consequential decisions changes the risk tier of the whole service.
Evidence requested: Feature list with automation level; configuration options

Question: Can the service explain individual outputs in terms a non-technical reviewer can understand?
Why it matters: Supports meaningful human review and individuals' rights to an explanation.

Question: Does the service disclose to end users and affected individuals when AI is involved or content is AI-generated?
Why it matters: Transparency duties apply to many AI systems regardless of risk tier.

Question: How do you monitor model performance in production, and what thresholds trigger investigation?
Why it matters: Models degrade as real-world data drifts away from training data.

Question: What is your process for releasing model updates, including re-validation and customer notification?
Why it matters: A model update is a material change to the service even when the API does not change.

Question: Can a model or AI feature be rolled back or disabled quickly if it behaves unexpectedly? When was this last tested?
Why it matters: A kill switch is the most basic AI incident control.

Question: Do you log model inputs, outputs and versions so that an individual decision can be reconstructed?
Why it matters: Without logs neither vendor nor customer can investigate a complaint. EU AI Act deployers must keep logs for at least six months.
Evidence requested: Logging specification; redacted sample log record

Question: Does your incident response plan cover AI-specific incidents such as harmful or biased outputs, data leakage through outputs and model misuse?
Why it matters: Traditional incident response plans focus on breaches, not on a model behaving badly.
Evidence requested: Incident response plan section; examples of AI incidents handled

Question: Within what timeframe will you notify customers of AI incidents affecting their data or decisions?
Why it matters: Notification clocks drive our own regulatory reporting.

Question: Will you contractually commit not to use our data for training without our written opt-in?
Why it matters: Turns a policy statement into an enforceable obligation.

Question: Will you provide the information we need to meet our obligations as a deployer (e.g. logs, instructions for use, bias test summaries)?
Why it matters: Deployer obligations depend on provider cooperation; secure it before signing.
